claims.text: The starting HEA protective coating has a well-developed FCC/BCC dual-phase microstructure.
The starting coating contains a distribution of FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
Coexistence of FCC and BCC phases creates numerous phase boundaries in the coating.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries impede dislocation motion during creep.
Impeded dislocation motion enhances the coating's creep resistance under sustained loading.
The governing structural mediator is the density and distribution of boundaries between FCC and BCC regions.
Phase boundaries obstruct dislocation glide during creep.
Phase boundaries obstruct dislocation climb during creep.
Obstruction of dislocation glide and climb slows plastic deformation and reduces long-term creep strain rate.
A dual-phase coating with abundant phase boundaries will accumulate creep strain more slowly than a homogenized or single-phase comparison coating.
A comparison coating with reduced phase-boundary features is expected to have a higher creep rate under identical loading conditions.
The proposed effect applies at temperatures high enough to activate dislocation-based creep.
The proposed effect is bounded to temperatures below those causing phase instability or dramatic microstructural coarsening.
The influence of phase-boundary density on creep resistance may depend on alloy composition, temperature, and applied load.
Grain-boundary sliding or diffusion creep may modulate the predicted phase-boundary effect.
The controlled comparison varies phase-boundary density while maintaining similar overall alloy composition and coating thickness.
Failure of the high-phase-boundary coating to show a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate relative to the uniform-microstructure control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
